page: Google Cloud Platform g2-standard-16 is a graphics-optimized virtual machine featuring a dedicated Intel Xeon processor with 16 vCPUs, consisting of 8 physical cores and 2 threads per core, running at 2.2 GHz. The system includes 64.0 GB of system memory, which equates to 4.0 GB per core, and is equipped with a single NVIDIA L4 GPU based on the Ada Lovelace architecture, providing 24 GB of dedicated VRAM. Local storage is not bundled with this instance type, and it does not include complimentary public IPv4 addresses.

Benchmark data indicates that the instance delivers top-tier performance, placing in the top 10% for large language model inference tasks on small and medium models in both prompt processing and text generation. In contrast, general CPU performance is more moderate, with single-core benchmarks and single-threaded compression tasks scoring in the bottom 25%. Multi-core CPU performance, memory bandwidth, and database operations fall consistently within the average range.

From a qualitative cost-efficiency perspective, the g2-standard-16 offers a specialized hardware profile that balances standard x86_64 compute resources with dedicated GPU acceleration. This makes it highly efficient for workloads that can offload processing to the NVIDIA L4 GPU, such as AI and machine learning inference, ray tracing, and image processing, while avoiding the higher cost of larger multi-GPU instances. It is best suited for medium-scale LLM inference, graphics rendering, and GPU-accelerated data science tasks.

It features an Intel Xeon x86_64 processor with 16 dedicated vCPUs, 64.0 GB of system memory, and a single NVIDIA L4 GPU with 24 GB of VRAM. The instance does not include local storage. Performance benchmarks reveal top-tier capabilities in LLM inference for small and medium models, while general single-core CPU performance and single-threaded compression tasks remain in the lower tier. Multi-core CPU performance, memory bandwidth, and database operations perform at an average level. This hardware profile offers a qualitatively cost-effective solution for GPU-driven tasks like machine learning inference, image processing, and ray tracing, though it presents tradeoffs for workloads requiring high single-threaded CPU speed or local storage.
